title: ATOD: Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation for Multi-turn Autonomous Agents

paper.title: ATOD: Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation for Multi-turn Autonomous Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Training small language-model agents for long-horizon interactive tasks requires both fast imitation and reward-driven improvement. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher guidance and typically improves rapidly in the early stage, but its gains saturate once the student approaches the teacher, limiting the final performance ceiling. Reinforcement learning (RL) directly optimizes environment rewards and encourages exploratory improvement toward a higher reward-defined ceiling, but sparse and delayed feedback makes early-stage learning much less efficient than OPD. In this paper, we propose ATOD ( A nnealed T urn-aware O n-policy D istillation), a hybrid online distillation algorithm that explicitly exploits this complementarity. (1) ATOD uses an annealed OPD–RL schedule : OPD dominates early training to approach teacher-level behavior, while RL is gradually strengthened to drive reward-based exploration. (2) ATOD introduces Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting ( T ​ - ​ DUR \mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} ), which softly amplifies high-utility turns and improves dense supervision in long trajectories. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA show that ATOD consistently outperforms competing post-training baselines: across the three student sizes, ATOD improves average success rate by 3.03 points over OPD and 23.62 points over GRPO, while surpassing the corresponding teacher models by 2.16 points.

Abstract Training small language-model agents for long-horizon interactive tasks requires both fast imitation and reward-driven improvement. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher guidance and typically improves rapidly in the early stage, but its gains saturate once the student approaches the teacher, limiting the final performance ceiling. Reinforcement learning (RL) directly optimizes environment rewards and encourages exploratory improvement toward a higher reward-defined ceiling, but sparse and delayed feedback makes early-stage learning much less efficient than OPD. In this paper, we propose ATOD ( A nnealed T urn-aware O n-policy D istillation), a hybrid online distillation algorithm that explicitly exploits this complementarity. (1) ATOD uses an annealed OPD–RL schedule : OPD dominates early training to approach teacher-level behavior, while RL is gradually strengthened to drive reward-based exploration. (2) ATOD introduces Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting ( T ​ - ​ DUR \mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} ), which softly amplifies high-utility turns and improves dense supervision in long trajectories. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA show that ATOD consistently outperforms competing post-training baselines: across the three student sizes, ATOD improves average success rate by 3.03 points over OPD and 23.62 points over GRPO, while surpassing the corresponding teacher models by 2.16 points. Figure 1 : Aggregate Qwen3-1.7B performance across ALFWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop. 1 Introduction Language agents extend large language models from static text generation to interactive decision making, where models must observe states, choose actions, call tools, and revise plans over multiple turns [ 1 , 2 ] . Such capabilities make LLMs applicable to embodied instruction following, web shopping, search-augmented question answering, code execution, and other real-world tasks [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . However, strong agentic behavior is usually concentrated in large models, whose inference cost and deployment overhead are undesirable in latency-, privacy-, and resource-sensitive settings. A practical goal is therefore to transfer multi-turn agentic competence from a stronger teacher to a smaller student, while still enabling the student to seek reward-driven improvements beyond pure teacher imitation. Reinforcement learning (RL) has been widely used for post-training language agents. It optimizes the policy with environment-defined rewards, typically through PPO- or GRPO-style policy optimization [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] , with recent agent-oriented variants adapting this idea to long-horizon interaction [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . More recently, on-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as another promising paradigm: it trains the student on its own sampled trajectories while using a stronger teacher’s token-level distribution as dense supervision [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . However, RL and OPD exhibit complementary trade-offs in multi-turn agent training. RL directly pursues environment rewards and can improve beyond imitation, but sparse delayed feedback makes early exploration inefficient for small students. OPD provides dense token-level guidance and bootstraps learning quickly, but strong imitation can plateau near the teacher and suppress reward-improving deviations. This motivates an annealed OPD–RL schedule: OPD dominates early training to approach teacher-level behavior, while RL is gradually strengthened to drive reward-based exploration. The validation dynamics in figure 2(a) illustrate this complementarity: OPD improves quickly but saturates, GRPO grows slowly under sparse rewards, and the annealed hybrid preserves the fast start while reaching a higher ceiling. (a) Training dynamics of ATOD, OPD, and GRPO. (b) T-DUR turn-utility weighting. Figure 2 : Motivation for ATOD. (a) Compared with OPD and GRPO, ATOD preserves OPD’s fast bootstrap while avoiding its plateau and GRPO’s slow sparse-reward learning. (b) T-DUR uses teacher–student divergence and student entropy to assign larger weights to high-utility turns. A second challenge concerns where dense teacher supervision should be applied within long agent trajectories. In multi-turn agent tasks, different turns can have very different learning value: prior agentic OPD studies show that inter-turn error compounding can push later states outside the teacher’s reliable support, making uniform trajectory-level supervision unstable, and that distillation strength should be adapted at the step level [ 20 , 21 ] . Meanwhile, token-importance studies in OPD suggest that student uncertainty and teacher–student disagreement identify informative distillation positions [ 22 , 16 ] . We therefore lift this idea from tokens to turns, because a turn is the natural decision unit of an agent trajectory. As visualized in figure 2(b) , entropy and disagreement vary substantially across turns; T ​ - ​ DUR \mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} estimates these signals from the log-probabilities of sampled tokens, avoiding full-vocabulary teacher sampling while efficiently assigning larger OPD weights to high-utility decision turns. We propose ATOD, short for Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation , to address these two challenges with an annealed OPD–RL schedule and Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting ( T ​ - ​ DUR \mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} ), as illustrated in figure 3 . Together, these components improve early convergence, stabilize dense supervision, and raise the reward-driven performance ceiling. Our contributions are three-fold: • We introduce an annealed OPD–RL training objective for multi-turn agent training. By letting OPD dominate early and RL dominate later, ATOD addresses the cold-start inefficiency of sparse-reward RL while preserving reward-driven improvement beyond pure teacher imitation. • We propose Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting ( T ​ - ​ DUR \mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} ), a soft distillation weighting mechanism for agentic OPD. T ​ - ​ DUR \mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} estimates turn-level distillation utility from student uncertainty and teacher–student disagreement, reducing wasted supervision on routine turns and emphasizing high-value decision points. • We validate ATOD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA across multiple student sizes. ATOD consistently outperforms competing post-training baselines, improves over both OPD and GRPO, and can surpass the corresponding teacher models. Figure 3 : Overview of ATOD. (a) Annealed guidance shifts from teacher-guided bootstrapping to reward-driven exploration. (b) T-DUR uses disagreement and uncertainty to upweight key turns, leaving rewards unchanged. 2 Related Work Language agents and tool-integrated reasoning. Language agents combine reasoning with action, enabling LLMs to interact with tools, environments, and external feedback [ 1 , 2 ] . Benchmarks such as ALFWorld, WebShop, and search-augmented QA require multi-step decision making under partial observations and delayed rewards [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . These settings differ from single-turn text generation because errors can propagate across turns and because many actions are routine while a few are decisive. Reinforcement learning for language models. Policy optimization methods, including PPO and GRPO, have been widely used to improve language-model reasoning and alignment [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Agent-specific RL methods further address long-horizon interaction through hierarchical multi-turn optimization, online curricula, group-in-group credit assignment, and adaptive exploration [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . GRPO is attractive because it estimates relative advantages within sampled groups without requiring a separate value model. However, in long-horizon agent tasks, sparse terminal rewards and high-variance exploration can make pure RL inefficient, especially for small models. On-policy distillation. OPD trains the student on its own generated trajectories while using a teacher distribution as dense supervision [ 14 , 15 ] . This reduces the train–test mismatch of offline supervised distillation and improves sample efficiency. Recent OPD variants improve stability, context transfer, entropy handling, or teacher-ceiling behavior [ 16 , 18 , 17 , 19 ] . For tool-using or multi-turn agents, recent work has explored step-wise, temporal, self-distilled, skill-conditioned, or importance-aware distillation to mitigate unreliable or redundant teacher signals [ 21 , 20 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 22 ] . ATOD is complementary: it combines OPD with reward-driven GRPO through a dynamic schedule and uses T-DUR to softly gate only the distillation component. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Multi-Turn Agent Trajectories We consider post-training a small language-model agent for multi-turn interactive tasks. Given an input x x , the student policy π θ \pi_{\theta} interacts with external feedback over K K steps. At step k k , the model generates a response a k a_{k} , which may contain reasoning, an environment action or tool invocation, or a final answer. If an external action is taken, an observation o k o_{k} is appended to the context and conditions subsequent generations.
